The shadow fleet helps Russia get around Western sanctions on its oil industry by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo.

European Union forces boarded a suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker in the Mediterranean earlier this week, according to Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief.

Troops from the bloc's Operation Irini boarded the MV Midag tanker on Friday and confirmed that the vessel was sailing under a false flag, Kallas said in a post on social media on Sunday.

"The EU will keep disrupting Russia’s shadow fleet at sea and through diplomatic means," she wrote, adding that EU foreign ministers were set to approve new sanctions against Russia on Monday, targeting "banks, buyers and companies supporting the shadow fleet."

Kallas also shared images appearing to show the boarding.

Russia uses its shadow fleet to evade Western sanctions on its oil industry. The shadow fleet gets around these restrictions by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo.

In August, Operation Irini forces carried out a flag verification boarding of the MV Sun oil tanker.

A similar mission also took place earlier in the month targeting the MV Toa Payoh ship.

Operation Irini was launched in March 2020 and was tasked with enforcing an UN arms embargo on Libya due to the Second Libyan Civil War.

Its original mandate was to counter illegal arms trafficking, gather information on oil smuggling, help disrupt human smuggling and train Libyan institutions responsible for law enforcement and search and rescue operations.

In October, Operation Irini's mandate was renewed through to 31 March 2029, with its objectives to include safeguarding the EU's interests in the Mediterranean and continuing to contribute to peace and stability in Libya.

One of its new responsibilities is also to help "constrain" Russia's shadow fleet, which it says uses the Mediterranean as a "key transit and transfer area."

Incumbent President José Maria Neves, who won the 2021 presidential election, is favoured to win a second term in office.

Cape Verdeans are heading to the polls on Sunday to elect the country's next president.

Incumbent President José Maria Neves, favoured to win a second term in office, comes up against five contenders, including Joana Rosa Amado, Cape Verde's first ever female candidate.

Voting starts at 8 am and polls will remain open for 10 hours. Provisional results are expected to come in overnight. If no candidate secures an absolute majority, there will be a second round on 29 November.

Amado, a 61-year-old lawyer backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy (MpD), is running under the slogan "Listen to Cabo Verde," which she says "does not mean promising everything, but rather, knowing the real concerns and expectations of the population."

"The election of a woman to the presidency would show many young women and young girls that no government job is barred from them," she told the media.

The former justice minister has centred her campaign on maintaining a balance of power, arguing that the country needs a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.

For his part, Neves, who won the 2021 presidential election with around 52% of the vote, has pledged to secure cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, as well as to create jobs and raise wages.

Between 2001 and 2016, the 66-year-old served as prime minister and president of the PAICV.

Among the other candidates is surgeon Gilson Alves, 45, an authoritarian figure who promises to fight corruption, allow gun ownership and restore the death penalty.

Cape Verde

Cape Verde sits off the coast of West Africa, around 600 km from Senegal. With roughly half a million inhabitants, it is known for its democratic stability, with a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections.

In July, Cape Verde was officially classified as an upper-middle-income country by the World Bank, due to economic growth in the tourism sector and a 16.8% increase in gross national income per capita between 2023 and 2024.

However, the country faces a number of challenges, including persistent social inequality, geographic isolation and a lack of affordable options for travel between its islands.

Among the main concerns of the local population are the rising cost of living, fuel prices and youth unemployment.

Cele mai puternice scăderi au fost înregistrate de companiile asociate direct cu dezvoltarea centrelor de date, precum producătorii de generatoare electrice și sisteme de răcire, dar și furnizorii de fibră optică, arată Financial Times. Prăbuşirea a șters aproape jumătate din creșterea de 9.400 de miliarde de dolari înregistrată de aceste companii în ultimele 12 luni, perioadă în care investitorii cumpărau masiv acțiunile firmelor care furnizează infrastructura necesară dezvoltării inteligenței artificiale.

În prezent, investitorii încep să se întrebe dacă dezvoltarea accelerată a inteligenței artificiale poate continua în același ritm, după o perioadă în care aproape orice companie conectată la această industrie a beneficiat de evaluări spectaculoase.

Caterpillar, unul dintre principalii furnizori de generatoare pe gaz pentru centrele de date, a pierdut 214 miliarde de dolari din valoarea de piață, echivalentul unei scăderi de -44% faţă de maximul istoric atins pe 30 iunie, potrivit datelor FactSet. La rândul său, compania de energie nucleară Oklo a pierdut -49% din valoare, în ciuda unui contract semnat cu Meta în ianuarie. În același timp, Comfort Systems, producător de sisteme de încălzire, ventilație și climatizare, și Corning, unul dintre marii producători de fibră optică, au pierdut fiecare aproximativ jumătate din capitalizarea bursieră.

Paul Kedrosky, investitor de capital de risc și cercetător afiliat MIT, consideră că pieţele au greșit atunci când au început să evalueze companiile industriale tradiționale ca și cum ar fi producători de semiconductori cu perspective de creştere accelerată. “Devenise o temă nesfârșită în discuțiile cu fondurile speculative și administratorii averilor familiale, această idee că absolut orice companie este acum una de creștere. Ceea ce este, desigur, ridicol”, a declarat Kedrosky.

Corecţia bursieră vine într-un moment în care investitorii sunt tot mai îngrijoraţi de cheltuielile uriașe ale giganţilor tehnologici pentru infrastructura AI, finanțate într-o măsură tot mai mare prin împrumuturi. În același timp, opoziția politică din SUA față de construirea unor noi centre de date ridică semne de întrebare cu privire la continuarea acestor investiții.

Aceste temeri afectează direct companiile industriale ale căror perspective de creştere au devenit tot mai dependente de extinderea infrastructurii AI. De altfel, din vară, sectorul industrial a avut a doua cea mai slabă evoluție din indicele S&P 500, după sectorul tehnologic.

Brett Ryan, economist senior pentru SUA la Deutsche Bank, consideră că evaluările multor companii au fost împinse artificial în sus de fluxurile masive de capital instituțional. “Au existat foarte multe investiții instituționale care s-au acumulat orbește în aceste tranzacții, alimentând probabil evaluări exagerat de optimiste pentru unele dintre aceste companii”, a explicat Ryan.

Economistul a explicat că, acum, piaţa bursieră începe să reflecte avertizările transmise deja de piața creditului, unde finanțarea tot mai riscantă a construcției de centre de date a ridicat semne de întrebare privind sustenabilitatea investițiilor.

Crowds outside the Texas Starbase erupted into cheers as the mechanical arms closed around the spaceship for the first time, a moment SpaceX said "changed everything."

The upper part of SpaceX's Starship rocket returned to Earth on Saturday, where it was caught between two mechanical "chopstick" arms in what marked the first-ever "catch" of a spaceship.

Starship had lifted off from Starbase in Texas on Friday before orbiting Earth 14 times as it deployed 26 satellites for Elon Musk's Starlink internet constellation.

After a 22-hour journey, the spacecraft approached Texas' east coast, with its three Raptor engines roaring into life as it broke through the clouds and began its descent back to the launchpad.

"Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement!" the company wrote in a post on social media alongside footage of the moment.

"I hugged ship 42 upon its return," SpaceX CEO Musk added in another post on X.

Crowds outside the Starbase erupted into cheers as the mechanical arms closed around the spaceship for the first time, a moment SpaceX said "changed everything."

Spaceships have previously been single-use vehicles, making each launch particularly expensive.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the catch "almost magic."

"Making more believers by the day," he wrote on X. Starship is lined up to serve as a landing system for NASA's Artemis Moon landing mission.

SpaceX had also attempted to guide a Super Heavy rocket booster back to the launch site shortly after Friday's launch. The effort was unsuccessful, however, with the booster "diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf." SpaceX has previously carried out three booster catches.

"The booster’s guidance, navigation and control triggered an automated abort during coast and diverted itself successfully to an offshore landing location," SpaceX said. It added that the boostback burn had "ended early due to low fuel mass" and that the root cause was under investigation.

The successful return of the rocket's upper stage was nevertheless a huge success for Musk and his company.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reportedly accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of misleading Kyiv over speed restrictions to its Starshield network.

Zelenskyy said on Thursday that Ukrainian forces were facing restrictions to the service, with terminals limited to a maximum speed of 161 kilometres per hour in areas occupied by Vladimir Putin's invading forces.

"The restrictions have now been in place for five days," the Ukrainian leader said in comments released on Saturday and reported by multiple outlets. "They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case."

The restrictions have been directly affecting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, Zelenskyy said in an address at the European Political Community summit in Dublin earlier this week.

"If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he told the summit.

On Friday, he added that Kyiv had received "no clear explanations" for the curbs.

"I instructed Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Minister of Defense to step up contacts with the U.S. Department of State, the Pentagon, and SpaceX to obtain clarification and resolve the situation," he wrote in a post on social media.

Starshield has proved critical to Ukraine's military operations against Russian forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

It came as Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to accelerate peace talks continue.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, per the AFP news agency.

Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.

"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.

A fragile Turkish delta and a melting Icelandic 'snow tree' are captured in the award-winning images.

From wildfire-scorched forests to algae-choked lakes, humans are leaving increasingly indelible marks on nature.

Carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels are pushing global warming towards and beyond the 1.5°C limit, resulting in ever worsening weather extremes.

Mass consumption is strewing coastlines with waste and polluting waterways with chemicals.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, and the European Environment Agency’s (EEA) latest state of the environment report found more than 80 per cent of protected habitats in poor or bad condition.

With the UN’s COP31 summit now in full swing, world leaders are coming together to get climate action back on track. Hot on the heels of the COP17 biodiversity talks, which ended on 31 October with a new roadmap but a UN report showing the world is falling behind on its 2030 nature goals, the intersection between nature and climate has been thrown into the spotlight.

It’s a relationship Europeans were invited to explore for this year’s EEA ‘Resilient by Nature’ photo competition.

Photographers from 35 countries set out to capture nature in states of harmony, disruption or renewal. From almost 2,800 entries, an external jury chose a winner in each category, as well as awarding a youth prize. The images were also put to a public online vote for the public choice award.

Harmony: Humans and nature find balance in Türkiye’s ancient delta

Türkiye’s Dalyan Delta has for decades stood strong against tourism development, with strict environmental protections helping to fight off resorts and other human activity.

Designated as a Special Environmental Protection Area in the 1980s, the ecologically vital wetland ecosystem is home to over 150 bird species and rare, endemic Turkish sweetgum forests.

Vulnerable loggerhead sea turtles nest on İztuzu Beach, where seasonal night closures and a ban on pets are in place to protect hatchlings.

Still, humans have long made their mark there: Lycian rock-cut tombs are carved into the cliffs along the delta’s labyrinthine channels, while the ruins of the ancient port city of Kaunos hark back to an era of maritime trading.

Now, eco-tourism, local fishing and wildlife preservation bring a slower pace to the delta – the delicate balance of which was captured from above by award-winning photographer Ali Aslan.

Disruption: A water rail wades through a rubbish-lined drainage pipe

Reminding us of what happens when humans neglect their duties of protection, Spanish photographer Julián Fernandez Quilez placed a remote-triggered, wide-angle setup inside a drainage pipe.

He captured a secretive wetland water rail wading through the murky, rubbish-filled pipe, probing a disposable medical face mask, bottle caps and a crushed drink can with its long red bill.

In the background, a watery habitat can be spied through the drain’s opening, putting into focus the consequences of human encroachment on natural ecosystems.

Renewal: A green shoot springs from a scorched landscape

Extreme heat and prolonged drought made 2026 among the worst years on record for wildfires, with nearly 700,000 hectares burned by August, according to the European Commission – nearly double the 20-year historical average.

The impacts are far-reaching: destroyed ecosystems and farmland, degraded soil, planet-heating emissions, health-harming air and water pollution that knows no borders.

While many of these landscapes will take decades to heal – and some will be changed irrevocably – Sofia-based photographer Elitsa Mihaylova reminds us of nature’s remarkable ability to heal.

Her image of a green shoot rising from the ashes appears “fragile, almost impossible, yet full of quiet strength”, according to the photo’s caption.

Youth Prize: Scat research and camera traps rewarded with rare sighting

Eighteen-year-old wildlife photographer Denat Lahi spends weeks mapping territories, photographing scat, and cross-referencing local wildlife databases in his home city of Lund, Sweden.

Lahi uses this intel to identify the best locations for capturing human-like emotion in mammals, he told photography news site PetaPixel.

His dedication has paid off: an image from his series following elusive pine martens in Sweden was awarded the Youth Prize by EEA.

Using nighttime camera trapping and motion-sensing, he snapped the curious creature exploring a dilapidated barn filled with industrial materials – a rare insight into the shy animals’ nocturnal forays into human environments.

Public Choice Award: Melting snow draws a ‘tree of life’ across Iceland’s highlands

Melting snow carves delicate lines in the Icelandic Highlands, with glowing green moss spreading like roots and branches. Barely perceptible from the ground, the scale and natural symmetry of the phenomenon is captured spectacularly by aerial landscape photographer Radoslav Sviretsov.

While snow in this northern wilderness naturally fades between May and June, warmer spring temperatures spurred by climate change are causing it to vanish earlier and earlier, while mild winters are hindering its ability to rebuild and disrupting water cycles.

Open to all European citizens and EEA member countries above 18 years old, the EEA photo competition is free to enter. It aims to bring light to the beauty of Europe’s nature, the environmental challenges it grapples with, and the solutions close at hand.

Whether it’s floating saunas in Norway or steaming thermal baths in Budapest, Europe offers travellers some spectacular spots to take on the winter chill.

Instead of retreating indoors to escape the winter chill, why not embrace it? Across Europe, thermal baths and outdoor saunas offer the perfect opportunity for wellness and to warm up.

Centuries-old bathing traditions and complexes remain a popular way to unwind across the continent.

So, if you’re looking to enjoy Europe's colder months in a different way, here are some warming places worth adding to your winter travel bucket list.

Thermal baths

Bathing beneath the aurora, Iceland

For Northern Lights chasers, Iceland’s Laugarás Lagoon combines geothermal bathing with the spectacular sights of the natural phenomenon.

The two-level lagoon on the banks of the Hvítá river is open well into the evening during winter and sits just over an hour's drive from Reykjavík. Visitors can enjoy aurora viewing at the backdrop of darker skies, when conditions allow.

The geothermal waters hover between temperatures of 37C and 39C, and, for a true Icelandic experience afterwards, visitors can brave the cold with a plunge in the pool, which is fed fresh river water.

Széchenyi Thermal Bath in Budapest, Hungary

Hungary’s capital Budapest is home to Széchenyi Thermal Bath, which is one of the largest spa complexes on the continent.

Its thermal section comprises three indoor pools, with the thermal water pool’s temperature ranging from 28C to 40C. Meanwhile, the outdoor thermal pool’s temperature is anywhere from 36C to 38C.

The water supply comes from the Saint Stephen Well Nr. II, which is made up of calcium, magnesium, and sodium, among other minerals. The mineral-rich waters are thought to be beneficial for supporting degenerative joint diseases as well as chronic and subacute arthritis.

Emser Therme in Bad Ems, Germany

Emser Therme offers an array of indoor and outdoor pools with temperatures between 18C and 38C. The indoor thermal pool hovers at 33C and features a small seating area with bubble jets. There is also a hot bubble pool and warmer indoor thermal pool at 36C.

At its Sidroga herbal steam bath, visitors are recommended to stay for no more than 15 minutes in the high humidity experience. It is set at 47C and has scents of camomile, sage, peppermint and thyme.

Its thermal water contains more than 30 minerals and trace elements. Emser Therme recommends no longer than a 20-minute stay in thermal water, accompanied by 20 to 30 minutes’ rest afterwards.

Bains Romains de Dorres in the French Pyrenees

At an altitude of 1,450 metres in the French Pyrenees, and offering sweeping views of the valleys, Bains Romains de Dorres has two outdoor pools where visitors can soak in waters heated to between 37C and 40C.

For those with muscle aches or pains, it recommends an hour’s soak in the baths for a soothing effect.

Thermae Bath Spa in Bath, England

One of the city’s most popular attractions, Thermae Bath Spa has four baths on offer at 35.3C, including an open-air rooftop pool with views of the skyline.

This spa is also home to the UK’s only day spa that features Bath’s natural thermal waters made of 42 minerals and trace elements – which were once enjoyed by the Celts and Romans more than 2,000 years ago.

Scenic outdoor saunas

Lakeside sauna at Alpenhotel Kitzbühel in Kitzbühel, Austria

For a view of Austria's Lake Schwarzsee while you unwind, check into Alpenhotel Kitzbühel and make a beeline for its lakeside sauna.

Located outside the hotel’s wellness area, the sauna is open year-round and temperatures can reach up to 90C.

Beyond the lake, visitors can also see the Wilder Kaiser mountain range and the Kitzbühel mountains.

Floating saunas in Aurland and Flåm, Norway

On the Aurlandsfjord in Norway, a sauna sits atop a floating dock surrounded by mountain views. Open three times a week during the winter season, FjordSauna offers a space that can accommodate up to 12 people. Visitors can book shared or private experiences, with a guided ritual available for the latter.

Sessions are no longer than one and a half hours, and alternate between steamy and cold fjord plunges.

In Flåm, evening "aufguss" rituals are a winter speciality. This is where a sauna master pours water mixed with essential oils onto the hot sauna stones alongside curated music. The guided session lasts 60 minutes for groups of up to eight people.

Archipelago sauna at Skärgårdens Kanotcenter, Sweden

In Resarö, Sweden, the crackle of firewood and hiss of steam comes with a sea view. The Skärgårdens Kanotcenter offers visitors one-and-a-half-hour sessions, where the sauna temperature ranges between 60C and 80C. Wood is provided on-site, for visitors to tend to the fire as they please.

Testul reprezintă un progres major pentru obiectivul dezvoltării unui sistem de rachete complet reutilizabil. Racheta a fost lansată vineri și, cu toate că propulsorul “Super Heavy” a explodat, partea superioară a ajuns pe orbită. După cel mai lung zbor al, în care a făcut de 14 ori înconjurul Pământului, a revenit la turnul de unde fusese lansată (Texas), fiind prinsă cu ajutorul unor brațe mecanice montate deasupra rampei.

A fost prima dată când compania SpaceX a lui Elon Musk a reușit să recupereze componenta principală a sistemului, care are o înălțime de aproximativ 52 de metri. În cadrul celui de-al 15-lea zbor de testare, 26 de sateliți Starlink au fost plasați pe orbită.

În privința booster-ului, sistemul de ghidaj a detectat că nu se află în poziție corectă și a declanșat protocolul de autodistrugere deasupra Golfului Mexic, a declarat Kate Tice de la SpaceX. Elon Musk a adăugat că Super Heavy nu avea nivelul necesar de combustibil. Inginerii încă investighează situația. Această treaptă de propulsie a mai fost recuperată de trei ori până acum.

NASA a salutat reușita, în condițiile în care investește miliarde de dolari în proiectele Starship și se bazează pe rachetă pentru misiunea Artemis de a readuce oameni pe Lună.
